summary: Positional language names WHERE things are relative to a landmark (on, under, behind, in front of, next to, above, below, left, right). Left/right, and behind/in front of when the landmark has no front of its own (e.g. a plain box), depend on viewpoint. Young children (4-6) perceive these relations early but describe them vaguely ('over there', with a point); the teaching job is to attach precise words to the concepts and model them in everyday talk as object + landmark + relation ('the ball is behind the sofa'). The deepest difficulties are holding two relations at once (dual relations) and left/right. Left/right for objects and for people facing you depends on viewpoint and is typically not mastered until early elementary school. Because this is a language-in-context topic, the core goal is productive AND receptive use: the child should both FOLLOW and GIVE positional instructions, not merely recognise words.
misconceptions: Uses vague deictic language ('over there', 'this one') with a gesture instead of a positional word
Judges left/right from the child's own current facing and cannot adjust it for an object or person facing the other way
Cannot hold two relations at once — a thing that is above one object and below another is described with only one relation (egocentrism / dual relations)
Treats a position as belonging to the object ('the front') rather than as a relation to a named landmark and a viewpoint

activities.title: Place the object: follow spoken positional instructions
steps: Listen to a spoken instruction naming an object, a landmark, and a relation, e.g. 'put the teddy behind the box'.
Move the named object into the correct relation to the landmark (for example drag it in a bedroom scene, or place a real toy with a real box and cup).
Try a short series that varies the relation: 'put the cup next to the teddy', 'put the pencil under the book'.
activities.insight: A positional word is an instruction that tells you exactly where to put something relative to a named landmark.

activities.title: Your turn to tell me: give the instruction (barrier / role-flip)
steps: Place or choose where a toy goes, then TELL a partner (adult, another child, or a cartoon friend) where it is using a precise positional word and a named landmark, e.g. 'behind the box'.
Have the partner act only on what the child says, so the child sees whether the word carried the meaning.
Play a barrier game: the child describes a hidden layout precisely enough for the partner to reproduce it without seeing it.
activities.insight: A position word is a tool that carries meaning to someone else — when I say the right relation and landmark, my partner can act correctly without seeing or pointing.

activities.title: In-role conversation: answering 'where is it?'
steps: Respond in role when a character asks 'where's the teddy?', answering with a positional word and landmark rather than a point.
Let the character act on the answer so the child hears whether it was clear.
Have the character gently model precise words by recasting vague answers ('over there' → 'yes, on the shelf next to the coat closet').
activities.insight: Everyday talk is where positional words become natural: naming the relation and landmark lets someone find or place a thing without seeing where you point.

activities.title: Build left and right on the body first
steps: Put a sticker on the right hand and use it as an anchor for 'left' and 'right'.
Play own-body directional games — shaking hands with the right hand, raising the left foot.
Later, try applying left/right to objects, with the adult expecting errors and not over-correcting.
activities.insight: Left and right start from my own body; applying them to objects and to people facing me is harder and comes later.

activities.title: Embed positional words in daily routines and games
steps: Set the table following and giving position talk: 'cups next to the plates, juice in the middle'.
Play directional games — hopscotch (forward/back) and board games with forward/back moves.
Describe everyday scenes — a set table, a shelf, a bedroom — naming object, landmark, and relation.
activities.insight: Positional words belong in everyday talk, not just lessons; using them in routines firms up the vocabulary over time.

checkQuestion: Set up a real or pictured scene with a box, a toy and a cup. Give a short series of doing-instructions and one telling task, and watch/listen for USE: 'Put the teddy behind the box. ... Now put the cup next to the teddy. ... Now YOU tell me where to put the pencil, so I can do exactly what you say.'
checkAnswer: Follows each positional instruction by placing the object in the correct relation, and, when giving the instruction, uses a precise positional word (behind / next to / on top of / under) together with a named landmark, so the teacher can act on it unambiguously — not a vague 'there' with a point.
